blocks.section: Catching up with a moving unit
blocks.source_markdown: A unit on the march does not wait for its orders. A Runner sent to it — to recall it, redirect it or change its [[stances|stance]] — is aimed at the point on its road where he can **catch up** with it, and the game tells you when he will. Runners are quicker than soldiers, but not endlessly: a recall or redirect that cannot catch the unit before it arrives still sends a Runner to its destination. For a newly sent land order, a missed meeting is not the end of the journey: if the unit has moved again, the Runner keeps the order and follows it along a new physical route. March, recall, redirect and stance orders take effect only when the Runner and the unit actually meet. The pending order says when its next meeting is expected and when it is following a new route. If it must wait before it can continue, the pending order says so without promising a delivery time. A Runner cannot deliver to a destroyed unit or one you no longer own.

blocks.source_markdown:
- **Where you found decides what you can make.** A catchment of plains and coast feeds people; one with a mountain may hold copper or silver. The [[founding]] forecast shows you the catchment before you commit.
- **Neighbours share ground.** Cities may be founded as close as **three** hexes apart, so their catchments overlap. A hex belongs to whichever city has [[citizens]] working on it; a neighbour cannot place anyone there while you hold it.
- **A held hex can be taken.** Stand one of your own forces on it in [[stances|fortify or sentry]], then place a citizen there. The holder's citizens go home to their idle pool, their building on the hex becomes yours at the same level, and any build they had queued there is cancelled and refunded. They are told by dispatch. A unit that merely marches through takes nothing, and if the holder has a unit standing guard there too, you must defeat it first ([[battle]]).
- **They can take it back** the same way: a unit in fortify or sentry, then a citizen placed.
- **A hex you have not scouted cannot be worked.** It is listed below the grid rather than drawn.
- **An enemy on your catchment hurts.** A hostile unit in [[stances|sentry]] on one of your hexes stops that hex feeding you. Hold enough of them long enough and a city falls without a battle — see [[sieges]].

blocks.source_markdown: The herd breeds itself — no herder is needed. Every ten animals give one calf every **5 game days** when the city has grain to feed it (**1 grain per calf**), and every **20 game days** on pasture alone. If the grain does not reach every calf, the fed ones come on the 5-game day beat and the rest wait for the 20-game day beat. A city can only keep so many animals: the **herd cap** is 50, and every level of a **Pen** ([[buildings]]) adds 100. **Status** and **City → Food** show it as *Herd 50 / 50*, with the next calves ("4 calves in 3 game days (4 grain)"). Each animal is worth **3 food**. Animals **above** the cap are eaten **first** at the game day's meal — fresh meat does not keep — and the four goods share whatever hunger is left. If animals are still above the cap after the meal, the pen cannot hold them and they are **lost**. A bigger Pen keeps more of them. Animals under the cap stay in the herd and are eaten only if the people would otherwise starve.

blocks.source_markdown:
- **Surplus, not store.** What counts is the daily balance — grain, fish, oil and wine produced, minus what the people eat — shown as the food *net* on the city. A positive net grows the city; zero or below holds it steady, even with full stores.
- **Surplus size.** A bigger surplus fills your stores faster; it does not itself raise the growth rate.
- **Variety.** Any one of the four food goods feeds people. Growth gains 10% per extra kind that forms a real share of the food eaten that game day, up to the existing variety ceiling: two substantial kinds give a 1.1 multiplier and four give 1.3. Livestock counts only if eaten as a real share of emergency food. A good merely sitting in store, or eaten only in crumbs, gives no variety bonus.
- **Size.** The city's walls set its ceiling: 2 000 people with no wall, then 5 000, 10 000 and 20 000 for a Palisade, Stone Wall and Bronze Wall ([[buildings]]). Growth runs at its full rate right up to the ceiling and then stops; a city at its ceiling never shrinks because of it. The city screen says "Walls hold N", and `keryx status` says it too.
blocks.status: planned; verify code and compact without dropping facts

blocks.source_markdown: In short: a city grows only while it makes more food than it eats; it holds steady when it does not; and it shrinks when it goes hungry. The city screen and `keryx status` say which of the three it is, and the food net behind it, for example "not growing: food net -1.7 per game day (needs more than 0)".

|---|---|

blocks.source_markdown: Any good can be offered, and wine and oil are offerings too ([[rites]]) — wine is also food, so a hungry city should keep it. For everyday prayers, incense can help meet the offering requirement, but more offering never improves the answer. For older prayers with uncertain answers, **a gift made mostly of incense can please the gods further than any other gift**: it raises the limit on what a larger offering can achieve. It never replaces your standing with the gods ([[kharis]]) — a god who does not hear you is not bought — but it is the best use of what you carry. Each god's taste is shown in the Offer row and in `keryx rite --list`; the gods of sight and omens love it most.

blocks.source_markdown: Bronze Age temples burned resin, not one perfume. Around the east of the Mediterranean the common kind was the sap of the terebinth tree (*Pistacia*), gathered on the dry hills of Kna'an and Cyprus and shipped in jars. The wreck at Uluburun, sunk off the south coast of Anatolia at the end of the thirteenth century before our era, carried about a hundred and fifty such jars among its copper and tin. Amphorae from Kna'an turn up in Egypt with traces of the same resin. The rarer frankincense and myrrh came to Egypt from Punt, far down the Red Sea, in small and precious loads; labdanum, scraped from the rock-rose shrubs of Crete, was the Minoan smell. Here they are all one good, **Incense**.

blocks.section: Arrange passage — send a ship for your own runner
blocks.source_markdown:
- **Sending one out:** the ship must stand in the SAME port the runner is waiting in. It sails straight for the runner's destination, boards it the moment it leaves, and puts it ashore there — no different from boarding any ship that happened to be going that way, except this one you chose yourself.
- **Bringing one home:** a runner that has finished its errand and is waiting in a **foreign** port may be fetched instead — any of your own ports will do. The ship sails there, waits (**War → Forces** shows it "waiting at (…) for the runner's return", or `keryx unit` says the same), and carries the runner all the way home the moment it is ready to travel.
- Either way, **the ship still finishes its own mission on its own** afterwards — it always sails home again, exactly like Land, Patrol or Explore. The runner never commands the ship; you send the ship for the runner, never the other way round. While it sails out, the drawer and `keryx unit` show it "carrying a runner to (…)".
- The ship's own risks are unchanged: it can still be damaged, captured or sunk, and a starved crew still turns it for home ([[upkeep]]) — none of that touches the runner, who stands safely ashore the whole time.

blocks.section: Fetch home — send a ship to fetch a unit
blocks.source_markdown:
- **The shore is chosen for you.** If the unit already stands on ground a ship can reach by sea, that is the shore. Otherwise the nearest open, unclaimed coastline near it is picked automatically — never a foreign city.
- **A runner rides along if one is needed.** When the unit does not already stand on the chosen shore, a Runner boards the very same ship, steps ashore with it, and marches inland to order the unit to the shore — exactly like [[messengers|arrange passage]]'s own crossing, just carrying a march order instead of a letter. Only a Galley or Emporos can carry that runner; a War Galley may only fetch a unit that is already standing on the shore.
- **The ship waits, but not forever.** You choose how many game days it holds off the shore. If the unit reaches the shore in time, it boards at once and the ship sails home with it. If the wait runs out first, the ship sails home empty — you are told either way.
- **Home is the end of the errand.** The moment the ship docks, the fetched unit steps off straight into that city's garrison — no separate Unload needed.
